CHAPTER 28 - NUTRITION AND HEALTH

Introduction

Good health is one of the most valuable possessions a person can have, and the food we eat is the single most important factor that keeps the body healthy, active and free from disease. This chapter explains what health and nutrition mean, describes the nutrients the body needs and what each one does, and shows how a balanced diet supplies energy and building materials in the right proportions. It then looks at what goes wrong when the diet is faulty - the deficiency diseases and the disorders of undernutrition and overnutrition - and finally at food adulteration and food preservation, two practical issues that decide whether the food on our plate actually nourishes us.

28.1 CONCEPT OF HEALTH AND NUTRITION

Health is not merely the absence of disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines HEALTH as "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." This broad definition reminds us that a healthy person is fit in body, sound in mind and able to live and work well in society.

NUTRITION is the science of food and its relationship to health. It covers the intake of food, its digestion, absorption, transport, assimilation and the way the body uses food to grow, repair tissues, obtain energy and stay well. A NUTRIENT is a chemical substance in food that the body needs for these functions. The main classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins and minerals, together with water and dietary fibre (roughage). Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are needed in large amounts and are called MACRONUTRIENTS; vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts and are called MICRONUTRIENTS.

28.2 NUTRIENTS AND THEIR FUNCTIONS

CARBOHYDRATES are the body's chief and cheapest source of ENERGY. They include sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose), starch and glycogen. On oxidation one gram of carbohydrate releases about 4 kilocalories (kcal) of energy. Good sources are cereals (rice, wheat, maize), potato, sugar and fruits. Glucose is the fuel that cells, especially brain cells, use directly. Excess carbohydrate is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles or converted to fat.

PROTEINS are the BODY-BUILDING nutrients. They are made of amino acids and are needed for the growth of new tissue, the repair of worn-out cells, and the making of enzymes, many hormones and antibodies. Proteins that supply all the ESSENTIAL amino acids (those the body cannot make) are called complete or first-class proteins; animal foods such as milk, egg, meat and fish provide them. Pulses, beans and nuts are good plant sources. One gram of protein yields about 4 kcal, but protein's main job is building, not fuel. Growing children, pregnant and nursing women need extra protein.

FATS AND LIPIDS are the most CONCENTRATED source of energy: one gram of fat releases about 9 kcal, more than twice that of carbohydrate. Fats provide and store energy, cushion and protect internal organs, insulate the body against cold, form part of every cell membrane, and carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Sources include ghee, butter, oils, nuts and oil-seeds. Fats are of two kinds - saturated (mostly animal fats) and unsaturated (mostly vegetable oils); too much saturated fat raises blood cholesterol and the risk of heart disease.

VITAMINS are organic substances required in tiny amounts that the body mostly cannot make for itself. They do not provide energy but are essential for regulating body processes; their absence causes specific deficiency diseases. Vitamins are grouped as FAT-SOLUBLE (A, D, E, K) and WATER-SOLUBLE (the B-complex and C).

Vitamin A (retinol) keeps the eyes, skin and mucous membranes healthy; it is needed for vision in dim light. Sources are milk, egg yolk, liver, and yellow-orange fruits and vegetables (carrot, papaya, mango) which contain carotene. Deficiency causes NIGHT BLINDNESS and dry eyes (xerophthalmia).

Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and phosphorus and so builds strong bones and teeth. It is made in the skin in sunlight and is found in egg, fish-liver oil and milk. Deficiency causes RICKETS in children (soft, bent bones) and osteomalacia in adults.

Vitamin E (tocopherol) is an antioxidant that protects cell membranes; sources are vegetable oils, nuts and green leafy vegetables. Vitamin K is needed for the CLOTTING of blood; it is found in green leafy vegetables and is also made by bacteria in the intestine. Its lack leads to delayed clotting and excessive bleeding.

Among the water-soluble vitamins, the B-COMPLEX group includes thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pyridoxine (B6), folic acid and cyanocobalamin (B12). They act mainly as co-enzymes in the release of energy from food and in the making of blood. Deficiency of thiamine causes BERIBERI (weak muscles and nerve damage); deficiency of niacin causes PELLAGRA (dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia); deficiency of folic acid or B12 causes a type of ANAEMIA. Sources of B vitamins are whole grains, pulses, liver, egg, milk and green vegetables. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is needed to make the connective tissue that holds cells together, to keep gums and blood vessels healthy and to help wounds heal; it is found in citrus fruits (lemon, orange, amla) and fresh vegetables. Its deficiency causes SCURVY, with bleeding, spongy gums and poor healing.

MINERALS are inorganic elements needed in small amounts for building tissues and regulating body functions. CALCIUM and PHOSPHORUS build bones and teeth; calcium is also needed for blood clotting, muscle contraction and nerve action. Milk and green leafy vegetables are rich in calcium; its lack weakens bones and teeth. IRON is part of haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood that carries oxygen; its sources are green leafy vegetables, liver, egg and jaggery, and its deficiency causes ANAEMIA, with tiredness and pallor. IODINE is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone thyroxine; its main source is iodised salt and sea food, and its lack causes GOITRE (swelling of the thyroid in the neck) and, in children, poor growth. SODIUM and POTASSIUM maintain the water and acid-base balance and help nerves and muscles work. Other minerals such as zinc, fluorine and copper are needed in trace amounts; fluorine, for example, protects the teeth against decay.

WATER makes up about two-thirds of the body. It is the medium in which all reactions take place, it transports nutrients and wastes, regulates body temperature through sweating, and keeps tissues moist. A person should drink plenty of water every day.

ROUGHAGE or DIETARY FIBRE is the indigestible part of plant food - cellulose from whole grains, vegetables and fruits. It adds bulk to the food, absorbs water, and helps the smooth movement of the bowels, preventing CONSTIPATION. Though it gives no nutrients, fibre is an essential part of a healthy diet.

28.3 BALANCED DIET AND THE FOOD PYRAMID

A BALANCED DIET is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the correct amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs for energy, growth, repair and protection. The exact requirement depends on a person's age, sex, body size, activity and physiological state (for example pregnancy).

The FOOD PYRAMID is a simple guide to a balanced diet. At its broad base are the energy-giving cereals and grains, to be eaten in the largest amounts; above them come fruits and vegetables (the protective foods rich in vitamins and minerals); then the body-building foods - milk, pulses, egg, meat and fish; and at the narrow tip, fats, oils and sugar, to be used sparingly. Eating according to the pyramid keeps energy and nutrients in healthy proportion.

28.4 ENERGY VALUE OF FOOD AND BMR

The CALORIFIC or ENERGY VALUE of a food is the amount of energy it releases when completely oxidised in the body, measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules. As a rule, 1 g of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal, 1 g of protein about 4 kcal, and 1 g of fat about 9 kcal. The energy content of a meal can be estimated by adding up these values for its components.

The BASAL METABOLIC RATE (BMR) is the energy the body spends at complete rest just to keep its basic processes going - the beating of the heart, breathing, maintenance of body temperature and the working of the organs. It is measured in a person lying at rest, awake, some hours after a meal. BMR is higher in growing children and in men, and varies with body size, age and the activity of the thyroid gland. Total daily energy need equals the BMR plus the extra energy used in physical activity; a labourer therefore needs far more food energy than a clerk.

28.5 MALNUTRITION

MALNUTRITION means "bad nutrition" - a disorder caused by a diet that is wrong in quantity or quality. It has two forms: UNDERNUTRITION, from eating too little food or too few nutrients, and OVERNUTRITION, from eating too much.

UNDERNUTRITION is common where food is scarce. The most serious form is PROTEIN-ENERGY MALNUTRITION (PEM) in children, which appears as two conditions. MARASMUS results from a severe shortage of BOTH energy and protein; the child becomes extremely thin and wasted, with a shrunken "old man" face, little muscle and no fat. KWASHIORKOR results mainly from a shortage of PROTEIN when energy (carbohydrate) intake is fair; the child shows swelling (oedema) especially of the belly and legs, stunted growth, thin discoloured hair and a puffy face. Both conditions leave children weak, prone to infection and poorly developed.

OVERNUTRITION, common where food is plentiful, leads to OBESITY - the excessive storage of body fat when energy intake exceeds energy spent. Obesity increases the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and joint problems. It is controlled by eating a balanced diet within one's energy needs and by regular exercise.

28.6 DEFICIENCY DISEASES

A DEFICIENCY DISEASE is caused by the lack of a particular nutrient over a long period. The important vitamin and mineral deficiency diseases are: SCURVY (lack of vitamin C - bleeding gums, poor healing); RICKETS (lack of vitamin D - soft, deformed bones in children); BERIBERI (lack of thiamine, B1 - nerve and muscle weakness); PELLAGRA (lack of niacin, B3 - dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia); NIGHT BLINDNESS (lack of vitamin A - poor vision in dim light); ANAEMIA (lack of iron or of folic acid/B12 - tiredness, pallor, breathlessness); and GOITRE (lack of iodine - swelling of the thyroid gland). Most of these are prevented simply by eating the foods that supply the missing nutrient.

28.7 NUTRITION IN DIFFERENT LIFE STAGES

Nutritional needs change through life. INFANTS grow fastest and are best fed on mother's milk, which is complete and protective. CHILDREN and ADOLESCENTS need plenty of energy, protein, calcium and iron for rapid growth. PREGNANT and NURSING women need extra protein, iron, calcium, folic acid and energy for the baby and for milk production. The ELDERLY need less energy but still need enough protein, calcium and vitamins, with easily digested food. Matching the diet to the life stage keeps each person well nourished.

28.8 FOOD ADULTERATION AND PRESERVATION

FOOD ADULTERATION is the deliberate lowering of a food's quality by adding a cheaper or harmful substance or by removing a valuable one - for example mixing chalk powder in flour, water in milk, or coloured leaves in tea. Adulterated food is less nourishing and may cause illness. In India the law (the Food Safety and Standards Act) protects consumers, and simple tests can detect common adulterants.

FOOD PRESERVATION is the treatment of food to stop it from spoiling so that it can be stored and used later. Food spoils mainly because of microorganisms (bacteria, moulds, yeasts) and enzymes. Common methods of preservation are: drying and dehydration (removing water so microbes cannot grow); refrigeration and freezing (slowing microbial growth by cold); heating and pasteurisation (killing microbes, as in boiling and canning); adding salt or sugar in high concentration (as in pickles and jam); adding chemical preservatives such as sodium benzoate; and canning and bottling in sealed containers. Preservation reduces waste and makes seasonal foods available all year.

28.9 ROLE OF NUTRITION IN HEALTH AND DISEASE PREVENTION

Correct nutrition is the foundation of good health. A balanced diet supplies energy and building materials, keeps the immune system strong so the body resists infection, and prevents both the deficiency diseases of undernutrition and the lifestyle diseases of overnutrition. Along with clean water, hygiene, exercise and rest, good nutrition is the cheapest and most effective way to stay healthy and to prevent disease.

SUMMARY

- Health (WHO) is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease; nutrition is the science of food and its use by the body.
- Nutrients are carbohydrates (energy, ~4 kcal/g), proteins (body-building, ~4 kcal/g), fats (concentrated energy, ~9 kcal/g), vitamins, minerals, water and roughage.
- Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K and water-soluble B-complex and C each have specific functions; their lack causes deficiency diseases (night blindness, rickets, beriberi, pellagra, anaemia, scurvy).
- Minerals such as calcium and phosphorus (bones, teeth), iron (haemoglobin), iodine (thyroxine) and sodium/potassium (balance) build tissues and regulate functions; their lack causes anaemia, goitre and weak bones.
- A balanced diet supplies all nutrients in correct proportions; the food pyramid is a practical guide, with cereals at the base and fats/sugar at the tip.
- Energy value: 4 kcal/g (carbohydrate and protein) and 9 kcal/g (fat); BMR is the resting energy expenditure, and total need = BMR + activity.
- Malnutrition is undernutrition (protein-energy malnutrition: marasmus from lack of energy and protein, kwashiorkor from lack of protein) or overnutrition (obesity).
- Food adulteration lowers food quality and can harm health; food preservation (drying, cold, heating, salt/sugar, chemicals, canning) stops spoilage.
- Good nutrition, with hygiene, water, exercise and rest, is the foundation of health and the prevention of disease.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Nutrition and Health (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For short-answer questions write 3-4 sentences; for long-answer questions write a full paragraph. Show working for any numerical (energy value) problems.

questions.question: Give the WHO definition of health and state why it is broader than 'the absence of disease'.
questions.answer: The World Health Organization defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' It is broader than the absence of disease because it requires a person to be fit in body, sound in mind and able to live and function well in society - a person free of illness may still be unhealthy if under mental stress or unable to cope socially.
questions.explanation: State the WHO definition and explain the three dimensions.

questions.question: Name the main classes of nutrients and state which are macronutrients and which are micronutrients.
questions.answer: The main classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins and minerals, together with water and roughage (dietary fibre). Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are needed in large amounts and are called macronutrients. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts and are called micronutrients.
questions.explanation: List nutrients; classify by amount needed.

questions.question: State the energy value of one gram each of carbohydrate, protein and fat, and calculate the energy in a food containing 30 g carbohydrate, 10 g protein and 20 g fat.
questions.answer:
Energy values: carbohydrate about 4 kcal/g, protein about 4 kcal/g and fat about 9 kcal/g.
Energy = (30 x 4) + (10 x 4) + (20 x 9) = 120 + 40 + 180 = 340 kcal.
So the food supplies about 340 kilocalories.
questions.explanation: Use 4/4/9 kcal per gram and add up.

questions.question: Match each vitamin to the deficiency disease it causes: vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin D, thiamine (B1), niacin (B3).
questions.answer: Vitamin A - night blindness (and dry eyes/xerophthalmia). Vitamin C - scurvy (bleeding, spongy gums). Vitamin D - rickets in children (soft, deformed bones). Thiamine (B1) - beriberi (nerve and muscle weakness). Niacin (B3) - pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia).
questions.explanation: Pair each vitamin with its deficiency disease.

questions.question: State the functions and deficiency effects of iron and iodine, and name one good source of each.
questions.answer:
Iron is part of haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood that carries oxygen; its deficiency causes anaemia (tiredness, pallor, breathlessness). A good source is green leafy vegetables (also liver, egg, jaggery).
Iodine is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre (swelling of the thyroid) and poor growth in children. A good source is iodised salt (also sea food).
questions.explanation: Iron -> haemoglobin/anaemia; iodine -> thyroxine/goitre.

questions.question: What is a balanced diet? Explain the food pyramid in one or two sentences.
questions.answer: A balanced diet is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the correct amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs. The food pyramid is a guide to it: cereals and grains form the broad base (eaten most), then fruits and vegetables, then body-building milk, pulses and meat, with fats, oils and sugar at the narrow tip (used sparingly).
questions.explanation: Define balanced diet; describe pyramid layers.

questions.question: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR) and state two factors that affect it.
questions.answer: The basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy the body spends at complete rest, awake, to keep its basic processes going - the heartbeat, breathing, maintenance of body temperature and the working of the organs. Factors that affect BMR include age (higher in growing children), sex (higher in men), body size, and the activity of the thyroid gland.
questions.explanation: Define BMR; give two influencing factors.

questions.question: Distinguish between marasmus and kwashiorkor, giving the cause and the main signs of each.
questions.answer:
Both are forms of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) in children caused by undernutrition.
Marasmus is caused by a severe shortage of BOTH energy (calories) and protein. The child becomes extremely thin and wasted, with almost no muscle or fat, a shrunken 'old man' face, and very low body weight.
Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by a shortage of PROTEIN when energy (carbohydrate) intake is fairly adequate. The child shows swelling (oedema), especially of the belly and legs, a puffy face, stunted growth, and thin, discoloured hair.
In short, marasmus is wasting from lack of energy and protein, while kwashiorkor is swelling from lack of protein; both leave the child weak and prone to infection.
questions.explanation: Marasmus = energy+protein lack, wasting; kwashiorkor = protein lack, oedema.

questions.question: What is food adulteration? Give two examples of common adulterants.
questions.answer: Food adulteration is the deliberate lowering of a food's quality by adding a cheaper or harmful substance, or by removing a valuable one, so that the food is less nourishing and may cause illness. Examples of common adulterants: chalk powder mixed in wheat flour, water added to milk, coloured leaves added to tea, or brick powder in chilli powder.
questions.explanation: Define adulteration; give two examples.

questions.question: Describe four methods of food preservation and explain how each prevents spoilage.
questions.answer:
Food spoils mainly because of microorganisms (bacteria, moulds, yeasts) and enzymes. Four methods of preservation:
1. Drying/dehydration - removing water so that microbes cannot grow (e.g. sun-dried grains, papad).
2. Refrigeration and freezing - low temperature slows the growth and activity of microbes and enzymes (e.g. frozen vegetables).
3. Heating/pasteurisation - heat kills microbes; boiling, pasteurising milk and canning preserve food.
4. Adding salt or sugar in high concentration - this draws water out of microbes and stops their growth (e.g. pickles preserved in salt, jam in sugar). Chemical preservatives such as sodium benzoate may also be added. All these methods stop or slow the microbes and enzymes that cause spoilage, so the food keeps longer and waste is reduced.
questions.explanation: Drying, cold, heat, salt/sugar; each stops microbial growth.

questions.question: Define nutrition and a nutrient.
questions.answer: Nutrition is the science of food and its relationship to health - it covers the intake, digestion, absorption and use of food by the body for energy, growth, repair and health. A nutrient is a chemical substance present in food that the body needs for these functions, such as a carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamin or mineral.
questions.explanation: Define nutrition and nutrient.

questions.question: Distinguish between macronutrients and micronutrients with examples.
questions.answer: Macronutrients are nutrients needed by the body in large amounts - carbohydrates, proteins and fats - which supply energy and building materials. Micronutrients are needed in only small amounts - the vitamins and minerals - and mainly regulate body processes. For example, carbohydrate (macronutrient) fuels the body while vitamin A or iron (micronutrients) are needed in tiny quantities to keep it working.
questions.explanation: Macro = large amounts (carb/protein/fat); micro = small (vitamins/minerals).

questions.question: State three functions of proteins.
questions.answer: Proteins are needed for (1) the growth of new tissue, (2) the repair of worn-out or damaged cells, and (3) the making of enzymes, many hormones and antibodies that defend the body. They are therefore called body-building nutrients.
questions.explanation: Growth, repair, and making enzymes/hormones/antibodies.

questions.question: State three functions of fats in the body.
questions.answer: Fats (lipids): (1) are the most concentrated store and source of energy (~9 kcal/g); (2) cushion and protect internal organs and insulate the body against cold; and (3) form part of every cell membrane and carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Sources include ghee, oils, butter and nuts.
questions.explanation: Energy store, protection/insulation, membranes and vitamin carrier.

questions.question: Why is roughage an important part of the diet even though it gives no nutrients?
questions.answer: Roughage (dietary fibre) is the indigestible plant material such as cellulose. Though it supplies no nutrients or energy, it adds bulk to the food, absorbs water and helps the smooth movement of the bowels, so it prevents constipation and keeps the digestive system healthy.
questions.explanation: Fibre adds bulk and prevents constipation.

questions.question: A person eats food containing 50 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 10 g fat. Calculate its total energy value.
questions.answer:
Using 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat:
Carbohydrate: 50 x 4 = 200 kcal
Protein: 20 x 4 = 80 kcal
Fat: 10 x 9 = 90 kcal
Total = 200 + 80 + 90 = 370 kcal.
So the food supplies about 370 kilocalories.

questions.question: Name the fat-soluble and the water-soluble vitamins.
questions.answer: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E and K. The water-soluble vitamins are the B-complex group (such as thiamine B1, riboflavin B2, niacin B3, B6, folic acid and B12) and vitamin C (ascorbic acid).
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B-complex and C.

questions.question: Describe the source, function and deficiency disease of vitamin D.
questions.answer: Source: vitamin D is made in the skin in sunlight and is also found in egg, fish-liver oil and milk. Function: it helps the body absorb calcium and phosphorus and so build strong bones and teeth. Deficiency: its lack causes rickets in children (soft, bent, deformed bones) and osteomalacia (softening of bones) in adults.
questions.explanation: Sunlight/egg/fish oil; helps Ca absorption; deficiency = rickets.

questions.question: Describe the function, a source and the deficiency disease of vitamin C.
questions.answer: Function: vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is needed to make the connective tissue that holds cells together, to keep gums and blood vessels healthy, and to help wounds heal. Source: citrus fruits such as lemon, orange and amla and fresh vegetables. Deficiency: its lack causes scurvy, with bleeding, spongy gums and poor wound healing.
questions.explanation: Connective tissue/gums; citrus/amla; deficiency = scurvy.

questions.question: Name the deficiency diseases caused by lack of thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3).
questions.answer: Lack of thiamine (vitamin B1) causes beriberi, marked by muscle weakness and damage to the nerves. Lack of niacin (vitamin B3) causes pellagra, marked by the 'three Ds' - dermatitis (skin), diarrhoea and dementia.
questions.explanation: B1 -> beriberi; B3 -> pellagra.

questions.question: What are minerals? Name any two important minerals.
questions.answer: Minerals are inorganic elements that the body needs in small amounts for building tissues and regulating body functions. Two important minerals are calcium (for bones, teeth, clotting) and iron (for haemoglobin); others include iodine, phosphorus, sodium and potassium.
questions.explanation: Inorganic nutrients; e.g. calcium and iron.

questions.question: Explain the function and deficiency of calcium in the body.
questions.answer: Calcium, together with phosphorus, builds and hardens the bones and teeth. It is also needed for the clotting of blood, for the contraction of muscles and for the normal working of nerves. Milk and green leafy vegetables are rich sources. A lack of calcium weakens the bones and teeth and can impair clotting and muscle/nerve function.
questions.explanation: Calcium builds bones/teeth, aids clotting, muscle, nerves; lack weakens bones.

questions.question: A person feels constantly tired, looks pale and gets breathless easily. Which mineral is likely deficient and what disease is this?
questions.answer: These symptoms - tiredness, pallor and breathlessness - are signs of anaemia, which is caused by a deficiency of iron (needed to make haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of blood). The person should eat more iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, liver, egg and jaggery.
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency -> anaemia.

questions.question: What is a balanced diet?
questions.answer: A balanced diet is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the correct amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs for energy, growth, repair and protection. The exact requirement depends on a person's age, sex, size, activity and physiological state.
questions.explanation: All nutrients in correct proportions for the body's needs.

questions.question: Explain the food pyramid as a guide to a balanced diet.
questions.answer: The food pyramid shows how much of each food group to eat. At the broad base are the energy-giving cereals and grains, to be eaten in the largest amount. Above them are fruits and vegetables (protective foods rich in vitamins and minerals). Next come the body-building foods - milk, pulses, egg, meat and fish. At the narrow tip are fats, oils and sugar, to be used sparingly. Eating according to the pyramid keeps energy and nutrients in a healthy balance.
questions.explanation: Cereals at base -> fruits/veg -> body-building -> fats/sugar at tip.

questions.question: Calculate the energy value of a meal of 40 g carbohydrate, 15 g protein and 12 g fat.
questions.answer:
Using 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat:
Carbohydrate: 40 x 4 = 160 kcal
Protein: 15 x 4 = 60 kcal
Fat: 12 x 9 = 108 kcal
Total = 160 + 60 + 108 = 328 kcal.
The meal provides about 328 kilocalories.

questions.question: What is malnutrition? Name its two forms.
questions.answer: Malnutrition means 'bad nutrition' - a disorder caused by a diet that is wrong in quantity or quality. Its two forms are undernutrition (from eating too little food or too few nutrients) and overnutrition (from eating too much food).
questions.explanation: Faulty nutrition; undernutrition and overnutrition.

questions.question: Compare marasmus and kwashiorkor.
questions.answer: Both are forms of protein-energy malnutrition in children. Marasmus is caused by a severe shortage of BOTH energy and protein; the child is extremely thin and wasted with an 'old man' face and no fat. Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by a shortage of PROTEIN with fair energy intake; the child shows swelling (oedema) of the belly and legs, a puffy face, stunted growth and thin, discoloured hair. So marasmus is wasting from lack of energy and protein, kwashiorkor is swelling from lack of protein.
questions.explanation: Marasmus: energy+protein lack, wasting; kwashiorkor: protein lack, oedema.

questions.question: What is obesity and what are its health risks?
questions.answer: Obesity is the excessive storage of body fat that occurs when the energy taken in as food is more than the energy the body spends. It results from overnutrition. Obesity increases the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and joint problems. It can be controlled by eating a balanced diet within one's energy needs and by taking regular exercise.
questions.explanation: Excess body fat from overnutrition; risks diabetes, BP, heart disease.

questions.question: What is food adulteration? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Food adulteration is the deliberate lowering of a food's quality by adding a cheaper or harmful substance, or by removing a valuable one, so that the food is less nourishing and may cause illness. Examples: mixing chalk powder in wheat flour, adding water to milk, or mixing coloured leaves in tea.
questions.explanation: Lowering food quality; e.g. chalk in flour, water in milk.

questions.question: Why does food spoil, and how does preservation prevent it? Give two methods.
questions.answer: Food spoils mainly because of the action of microorganisms (bacteria, moulds, yeasts) and of enzymes in the food. Preservation treats the food to stop or slow these agents so it keeps longer. Two methods: (1) drying/dehydration removes the water that microbes need to grow; (2) refrigeration or freezing uses cold to slow the growth of microbes and enzyme action. Other methods include heating (pasteurisation/canning), salting or sugaring, and chemical preservatives.
questions.explanation: Spoilage by microbes/enzymes; drying and cold prevent it.

questions.question: How do the nutritional needs of a pregnant woman and an elderly person differ?
questions.answer: A pregnant (and nursing) woman needs EXTRA protein, iron, calcium, folic acid and energy to support the growth of the baby and the making of milk. An elderly person needs LESS total energy because activity and metabolism are lower, but still needs enough protein, calcium and vitamins in easily digested form to maintain the body and prevent bone loss. Thus the diet is matched to each life stage.
questions.explanation: Pregnancy: extra protein/iron/calcium/energy; elderly: less energy, easily digested food.

questions.question: Explain the concept of health and nutrition, and describe the main classes of nutrients and their broad roles.
questions.answer:
Health, as defined by the World Health Organization, is 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' A healthy person is fit in body, sound in mind and able to live and work well in society. Nutrition is the science of food and its relationship to health; it covers how food is taken in, digested, absorbed and used by the body for energy, growth, repair and protection. A nutrient is a food chemical the body needs for these purposes.
The main classes of nutrients are:
1. Carbohydrates - the chief, cheapest source of energy (~4 kcal/g), from cereals, sugar and fruit.
2. Proteins - the body-building nutrients (~4 kcal/g), made of amino acids, needed for growth, repair, enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
3. Fats - the most concentrated energy source (~9 kcal/g), which also store energy, protect organs and carry fat-soluble vitamins.
4. Vitamins - organic substances needed in tiny amounts to regulate processes; their lack causes deficiency diseases.
5. Minerals - inorganic elements for building tissues and regulating functions.
6. Water - about two-thirds of the body, the medium of all reactions and of transport and temperature control.
7. Roughage - indigestible fibre that adds bulk and prevents constipation.
Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are macronutrients (large amounts); vitamins and minerals are micronutrients (small amounts). Together, in correct proportion, they keep the body healthy.
questions.explanation: Health (WHO) + nutrition; list and role of each nutrient class.

questions.question: Describe carbohydrates, proteins and fats - their functions, food sources and energy values.
questions.answer:
Carbohydrates are the body's chief and cheapest source of energy. They include sugars, starch and glycogen and give about 4 kcal per gram. Sources are cereals (rice, wheat, maize), potato, sugar and fruits. Glucose is the fuel cells use directly, and excess is stored as glycogen or fat.
Proteins are the body-building nutrients, made of amino acids. They are needed for the growth of new tissue, the repair of cells, and the making of enzymes, hormones and antibodies. They give about 4 kcal per gram but their main job is building, not fuel. Complete (first-class) proteins from milk, egg, meat and fish supply all essential amino acids; pulses, beans and nuts are good plant sources.
Fats (lipids) are the most concentrated energy source, giving about 9 kcal per gram - more than twice carbohydrate. They provide and store energy, cushion and protect organs, insulate against cold, form part of cell membranes and carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Sources are ghee, butter, oils, nuts and oil-seeds. Too much saturated (animal) fat raises blood cholesterol and heart-disease risk. Thus the three macronutrients together supply the body's energy and building needs.
questions.explanation: Functions, sources and energy values of carbohydrate, protein and fat.

questions.question: Classify vitamins and describe, for any four vitamins, their source, function and deficiency disease.
questions.answer:
Vitamins are organic substances needed in tiny amounts to regulate body processes; the body cannot make most of them. They are grouped as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B-complex and C).
1. Vitamin A - source: milk, egg yolk, liver and yellow-orange fruits/vegetables (carrot, papaya). Function: keeps eyes, skin and mucous membranes healthy and enables vision in dim light. Deficiency: night blindness and dry eyes.
2. Vitamin D - source: sunlight on the skin, egg, fish-liver oil, milk. Function: helps absorb calcium and phosphorus for strong bones and teeth. Deficiency: rickets in children.
3. Vitamin C - source: citrus fruits, amla, fresh vegetables. Function: makes connective tissue, keeps gums and blood vessels healthy, helps healing. Deficiency: scurvy (bleeding gums).
4. Thiamine (B1) - source: whole grains, pulses, liver. Function: a co-enzyme in releasing energy from food. Deficiency: beriberi (nerve and muscle weakness).
(Others: niacin B3 lack causes pellagra; vitamin K is needed for blood clotting; folic acid/B12 lack causes anaemia.) Each vitamin therefore has a specific role, and its absence produces a characteristic deficiency disease that is prevented simply by eating the right foods.
questions.explanation: Fat/water-soluble classes; four vitamins with source, function, deficiency.

questions.question: Describe the functions, sources and deficiency effects of calcium, iron and iodine.
questions.answer:
Minerals are inorganic elements needed in small amounts for building tissues and regulating body functions.
Calcium: with phosphorus it builds and hardens bones and teeth, and it is also needed for the clotting of blood, the contraction of muscles and the working of nerves. Sources: milk and green leafy vegetables. Deficiency: weak, soft bones and teeth and impaired clotting and muscle/nerve action.
Iron: it is part of haemoglobin, the red pigment of blood that carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. Sources: green leafy vegetables, liver, egg and jaggery. Deficiency: anaemia, with tiredness, pallor and breathlessness.
Iodine: it is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism. Sources: iodised salt and sea food. Deficiency: goitre (swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck) and, in children, poor physical and mental growth.
Thus each mineral has a definite function, and its lack produces a specific disorder that is prevented by eating mineral-rich foods or, for iodine, using iodised salt.
questions.explanation: Calcium (bones), iron (haemoglobin), iodine (thyroxine); sources and deficiencies.

questions.question: Explain the balanced diet and the food pyramid, and estimate the energy value of a day's food containing 300 g carbohydrate, 80 g protein and 60 g fat.
questions.answer:
A balanced diet contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the correct amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs for energy, growth, repair and protection. The needs vary with age, sex, size, activity and physiological state.
The food pyramid is a practical guide: energy-giving cereals form the broad base (eaten most); above them are protective fruits and vegetables; then body-building milk, pulses, egg and meat; and at the narrow tip fats, oils and sugar, used sparingly. Eating according to the pyramid keeps the diet balanced.
Energy estimate (using 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat):
Carbohydrate: 300 x 4 = 1200 kcal
Protein: 80 x 4 = 320 kcal
Fat: 60 x 9 = 540 kcal
Total = 1200 + 320 + 540 = 2060 kcal.
So the day's food supplies about 2060 kilocalories - close to the daily need of a moderately active adult.
questions.explanation: Define balanced diet and pyramid; energy = 1200+320+540 = 2060 kcal.

questions.question: Explain malnutrition. Distinguish undernutrition from overnutrition and describe marasmus, kwashiorkor and obesity.
questions.answer:
Malnutrition means 'bad nutrition' - a disorder caused by a diet wrong in quantity or quality. It has two forms.
Undernutrition arises from eating too little food or too few nutrients and is common where food is scarce. Its most serious form is protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) in children:
- Marasmus results from a severe shortage of BOTH energy and protein; the child becomes extremely thin and wasted, with a shrunken 'old man' face, almost no muscle or fat, and very low weight.
- Kwashiorkor results mainly from a shortage of PROTEIN while energy intake is fair; the child shows swelling (oedema), especially of the belly and legs, a puffy face, stunted growth and thin, discoloured hair.
Overnutrition arises from eating too much, common where food is plentiful, and leads to obesity - the excessive storage of body fat when energy intake exceeds energy spent. Obesity raises the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and joint problems.
Both extremes harm health: undernutrition leaves children weak and prone to infection, while overnutrition brings lifestyle diseases. A balanced diet matched to one's energy needs, with exercise, prevents both.
questions.explanation: Under vs over; marasmus, kwashiorkor, obesity described.

questions.question: Describe food adulteration and the main methods of food preservation, and explain why preservation is useful.
questions.answer:
Food adulteration is the deliberate lowering of a food's quality by adding a cheaper or harmful substance, or by removing a valuable one - for example mixing chalk powder in flour, adding water to milk, or putting coloured leaves in tea. Adulterated food is less nourishing and may cause illness; laws such as the Food Safety and Standards Act and simple tests help protect consumers.
Food preservation is the treatment of food to stop it spoiling so it can be stored and used later. Food spoils mainly because of microorganisms (bacteria, moulds, yeasts) and enzymes. The main methods are:
1. Drying/dehydration - removing water so microbes cannot grow.
2. Refrigeration and freezing - cold slows microbial growth and enzyme action.
3. Heating/pasteurisation - heat kills microbes (boiling, canning, pasteurising milk).
4. Salting or sugaring - high salt or sugar draws water out of microbes (pickles, jam).
5. Chemical preservatives - substances such as sodium benzoate.
6. Canning and bottling in sealed containers.
Preservation is useful because it reduces wastage of food, keeps food safe from spoilage and infection, and makes seasonal foods available throughout the year.
questions.explanation: Adulteration lowers quality; preservation methods stop spoilage and reduce waste.

questions.question: Define BMR and explain how total daily energy needs are worked out. Why does a labourer need more food than an office clerk?
questions.answer:
The basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy the body spends at complete rest, awake, some hours after a meal, simply to keep its basic life processes going - the heartbeat, breathing, maintenance of body temperature and the working of the organs. BMR varies with age (higher in growing children), sex (higher in men), body size and the activity of the thyroid gland.
The total daily energy requirement of a person is the BMR PLUS the extra energy used for physical activity (and, in children and pregnant women, for growth). So total energy need = BMR + activity energy.
A manual labourer does heavy physical work, which uses a large amount of extra energy on top of the BMR, whereas an office clerk sits most of the day and uses little extra energy. Therefore, even if their BMRs are similar, the labourer's total daily energy need is much greater, and he must eat more food (more kilocalories) to meet it. If either eats far more or far less than needed, malnutrition (obesity or wasting) results.
questions.explanation: BMR = resting energy; total = BMR + activity; labourer's activity is high.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The World Health Organization defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' Nutrition is the science of food and its use by the body, and the nutrients it studies are classed as macronutrients and micronutrients.
(a) Give the WHO definition of health.
(b) What is meant by nutrition?
(c) Name the macronutrients and the micronutrients.
(d) Why can a person free of disease still be called unhealthy?
questions.answer:
(a) Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
(b) Nutrition is the science of food and its relationship to health - how food is taken in, digested, absorbed and used by the body.
(c) Macronutrients: carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Micronutrients: vitamins and minerals.
(d) Because health also requires mental and social well-being; a person with no disease may still be unhealthy if under mental stress or unable to function socially.
questions.explanation: WHO definition; nutrition; macro/micro; three dimensions of health.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The three macronutrients supply the body's energy and building materials. On oxidation, 1 g of carbohydrate or protein gives about 4 kcal, while 1 g of fat gives about 9 kcal. A student's lunch contains 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat.
(a) Which nutrient gives the most energy per gram?
(b) Calculate the energy from the carbohydrate in the lunch.
(c) Find the total energy value of the lunch.
(d) Which macronutrient is mainly for body-building rather than energy?
questions.answer:
(a) Fat gives the most energy per gram (about 9 kcal/g).
(b) Carbohydrate energy = 60 x 4 = 240 kcal.
(c) Total = (60x4) + (20x4) + (15x9) = 240 + 80 + 135 = 455 kcal.
(d) Protein is mainly for body-building (growth and repair).
questions.explanation: Fat densest; carb 240 kcal; total 455 kcal; protein builds body.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A school medical camp finds several children with signs of vitamin deficiency: one child cannot see well in dim light, another has bleeding, spongy gums, and a third has soft, bent leg bones.
(a) Which vitamin does the first child lack, and what is the disease?
(b) Which vitamin does the second child lack, and what is the disease?
(c) Which vitamin does the third child lack, and what is the disease?
(d) Suggest one food to correct each deficiency.
questions.answer:
(a) The first child lacks vitamin A - the condition is night blindness.
(b) The second child lacks vitamin C - the condition is scurvy.
(c) The third child lacks vitamin D - the condition is rickets.
(d) Vitamin A: carrot/papaya (or milk, liver); vitamin C: orange/amla; vitamin D: sunlight, egg or fish-liver oil (with milk for calcium).
questions.explanation: Vitamin A/night blindness; C/scurvy; D/rickets; matching foods.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Minerals are inorganic nutrients with specific roles: iron is part of haemoglobin, iodine is used by the thyroid gland to make thyroxine, and calcium builds bones and teeth. In a village, many people show tiredness and pallor, and some have a visible swelling in the neck.
(a) Which mineral deficiency causes tiredness and pallor, and what is the disease?
(b) Which mineral deficiency causes the neck swelling, and what is the disease?
(c) Suggest a simple measure to prevent the neck swelling in the village.
(d) Name one function of calcium other than building bones.
questions.answer:
(a) Iron deficiency causes tiredness and pallor - the disease is anaemia.
(b) Iodine deficiency causes the neck swelling - the disease is goitre (enlarged thyroid).
(c) Use iodised salt in cooking (and include sea food) to supply iodine.
(d) Calcium is also needed for the clotting of blood (or for muscle contraction / nerve action).
questions.explanation: Iron/anaemia; iodine/goitre; iodised salt; calcium clotting.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A balanced diet supplies all nutrients in correct proportions. Energy values are 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate and protein and 9 kcal/g for fat. A dietician plans a meal of 45 g carbohydrate, 25 g protein and 20 g fat.
(a) What is a balanced diet?
(b) Calculate the energy from each nutrient in the meal.
(c) Find the total energy value of the meal.
(d) In the food pyramid, which foods are eaten in the largest amount?
questions.answer:
(a) A balanced diet contains all nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the correct amounts and proportions for the body's needs.
(b) Carbohydrate: 45 x 4 = 180 kcal; protein: 25 x 4 = 100 kcal; fat: 20 x 9 = 180 kcal.
(c) Total = 180 + 100 + 180 = 460 kcal.
(d) The energy-giving cereals and grains at the base of the pyramid are eaten in the largest amount.
questions.explanation: Balanced diet; 180/100/180; total 460 kcal; cereals at base.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Protein-energy malnutrition affects children fed a poor diet. In a clinic, one child is extremely thin and wasted with an 'old man' face, while another has swelling of the belly and legs with thin, discoloured hair.
(a) Name the condition of the first child and its cause.
(b) Name the condition of the second child and its cause.
(c) To which group of disorders do both belong?
(d) State one general effect of these conditions on the child's health.
questions.answer:
(a) The first child has marasmus, caused by a severe shortage of both energy and protein.
(b) The second child has kwashiorkor, caused mainly by a shortage of protein (with fair energy intake).
(c) Both belong to protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), a form of undernutrition.
(d) The child becomes weak, grows poorly and is prone to infections (any one).
questions.explanation: Marasmus (energy+protein); kwashiorkor (protein); PEM; weakness/infection.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In cities where food is plentiful, overnutrition is common. A man eats far more energy-rich food than his body uses and takes little exercise; over the years he stores a large amount of body fat.
(a) What disorder is he developing, and to which type of malnutrition does it belong?
(b) Name two diseases whose risk it increases.
(c) Why does storing fat occur here?
(d) Suggest two measures to control the condition.
questions.answer:
(a) He is developing obesity, which belongs to overnutrition (a form of malnutrition).
(b) It increases the risk of diabetes and high blood pressure (also heart disease and joint problems).
(c) Fat is stored because his energy intake from food is more than the energy his body spends, and the excess is laid down as body fat.
(d) Eat a balanced diet within his energy needs (less fat and sugar) and take regular exercise.
questions.explanation: Obesity/overnutrition; diabetes and BP; intake > expenditure; diet + exercise.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Food safety involves two issues. Food adulteration lowers a food's quality, while food preservation stops food from spoiling. Common adulterants include chalk in flour and water in milk; common preservation methods include drying, cooling, heating and salting.
(a) Define food adulteration.
(b) Give two examples of adulterants.
(c) How does drying preserve food?
(d) Name two other methods of preservation.
questions.answer:
(a) Food adulteration is the deliberate lowering of a food's quality by adding a cheaper or harmful substance, or removing a valuable one.
(b) Examples: chalk powder in wheat flour and water added to milk (also coloured leaves in tea).
(c) Drying removes the water that microbes need to grow, so the food does not spoil.
(d) Two other methods: refrigeration/freezing and heating/pasteurisation (also salting/sugaring, chemical preservatives, canning).
questions.explanation: Adulteration definition; examples; drying removes water; other methods.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy the body uses at complete rest to keep its basic processes going. The total daily energy need is the BMR plus the energy used for physical activity. Two men have the same BMR, but one is a farmer doing heavy work and the other is an office clerk.
(a) Define BMR.
(b) Write the relation between total daily energy need, BMR and activity.
(c) Which man needs more food energy, and why?
(d) Name one factor, other than activity, that affects BMR.
questions.answer:
(a) BMR is the energy the body spends at complete rest, awake, to maintain basic life processes such as heartbeat, breathing and body temperature.
(b) Total daily energy need = BMR + energy used for physical activity.
(c) The farmer needs more food energy, because his heavy physical work uses much more activity energy on top of the same BMR.
(d) Age (or sex, body size, thyroid activity) affects BMR - any one.
questions.explanation: BMR defined; total = BMR + activity; farmer needs more; age/thyroid.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Vitamins are needed in tiny amounts and are grouped as fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B-complex and C). Vitamin K helps blood to clot, thiamine (B1) prevents beriberi and niacin (B3) prevents pellagra.
(a) On what basis are vitamins classified into two groups?
(b) Which vitamin is needed for the clotting of blood?
(c) Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra?
(d) Name the disease caused by lack of thiamine (B1).
questions.answer:
(a) Vitamins are classified by their solubility - fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fat, and water-soluble (B-complex and C) dissolve in water.
(b) Vitamin K is needed for the clotting of blood.
(c) Pellagra is caused by the deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3).
(d) Lack of thiamine (vitamin B1) causes beriberi.
questions.explanation: Classified by solubility; K clotting; niacin/pellagra; B1/beriberi.
